chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Yazid ibn Khalifa who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Umar ibn Hanzala came to us from you with the (prayer) timings. He said: So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Then he would not have lied against us.'

I said: He said the time for Maghrib is when the disc (of the sun) disappears, except that the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) used to, when the journey was pressing upon him, delay the Maghrib and combine it with the Isha. So he (the Imam) said: 'He spoke the truth.'
And he said: 'The time for Isha is when the twilight disappears until a third of the night, and the time for Fajr is when it (the dawn) appears until it brightens.'

key_terms.الشَّفَقُ: Twilight/redness — the reddish glow of the horizon after sunset; its disappearance marks Isha
key_terms.الْقُرْصُ: The disc — refers to the sun's disc; its disappearance marks the entry of Maghrib
key_terms.جَدَّ بِهِ السَّيْرُ: The journey was pressing upon him — idiom for a difficult or hurried journey requiring combined prayers
key_terms.وَقْتُ الْمَغْرِبِ: Time for Maghrib — begins at true sunset (disappearance of the sun's disc)

ai.seo_question: When does the time for Maghrib, Isha, and Fajr begin according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) confirmed a report brought by Umar ibn Hanzala about the times for Maghrib, Isha, and Fajr prayers. The Imam affirmed that Maghrib begins at sunset (when the sun's disc disappears), while granting an exception for travel — when the journey is pressing, the Prophet (SAWW) combined Maghrib and Isha. Isha's time runs from the disappearance of the evening redness to one-third of the night, while Fajr's time is from the first appearance of dawn's light until full brightness. This hadith also demonstrates the Imam's endorsement of reliable transmitters like Umar ibn Hanzala, whose report he validated without hesitation.
